The book

The Autonomous Enterprise

How Leaders Build, Govern, and Scale the Agent-Run Company. 31 chapters, 742 pages, first edition November 2026.

The management problem

Agents can act. Who decides how far?

Every large company hears the same promise: agents that close the books, chase invoices, buy materials and resolve tickets with little human effort.

But companies run several ERPs, a mainframe, CRM, HR and procurement suites, and hundreds of interfaces built over twenty years.

Three questions

  1. Who decides where an agent can act?
  2. Who owns a decision that spans five systems and three departments?
  3. Who explains it to the auditor and the board?

The answer: five decisions leaders own

  1. Where agents act. Start from an outcome Finance can measure, then use the simplest engine that works: rules, models or solvers before agents. Book, Ch 21.3 Which step goes where
  2. How far they’re trusted. Set a level per step, L0 to L5. Promotion is earned on evidence and decided by a named body; demotion is automatic. Book, Ch 01.5 Who sets the level
  3. Who answers. Every agent has a named business owner who signs its limits and promotions and can stop it. No registry, no run. Book, Ch 24.3 Agents are owned, not managed
  4. How you stop them. The harness enforces limits and budgets. Irreversible steps stay behind human gates, and a tested kill switch stops one agent or the fleet. Book, Ch 05.8 The kill switch
  5. Whether it pays. Compare agents in cost per completed outcome, track each agent’s net contribution, and run pilots that end in a decision. Book, Ch 25.4 Cost per outcome

The frameworks give agents the ability to act. Leadership decides how far they’re trusted.

The capstone, as a storyboard

One order, end to end

The book ends by following one made-to-order order through every system at month 30 of the plan. Agents do the work. People sign where the book says they must. Book, Ch 30

  1. 1

    Intake agent · L3

    The order arrives

    The customer’s buying agent sends an order for four pump skids, USD 186,400. Only named partners may order this way. No person touches it.

  2. 2

    Price, credit, promise

    Confirmed in 39 minutes

    The agent prices from the contract. A credit rule releases the order. The promise agent offers July 30. In 2026 this took 4 days.

  3. 3

    Buy-out agent · L3

    The missing part is bought

    The agent orders four drive panels under a frame contract on day 0, not day 6. Supplier bank changes always go to a person.

  4. 4

    Production agent · L3

    The plant builds

    The agent releases the order to the plant. A gasket set fails and is replaced inside the plan’s float. The agent does nothing, and the trace records that.

  5. 5

    Quality · a person signs

    The agent stops

    The quality agent builds the evidence pack, then stops. A qualified inspector witnesses the last test and signs. The agent may prepare the release, not give it.

  6. 6

    Billing agent · L3

    Delivery triggers the invoice

    Proof of delivery creates the invoice. An anomaly gate scores it normal. One line is wrong: the contract says the company pays the freight.

  7. 7

    Dispute agent · L2 over the limit

    Fixed in one day, not 38

    The customer short-pays USD 3,450. The claim clears the threshold: 0.96 against 0.81. The amount is over the USD 2,500 limit, so a credit manager approves.

  8. 8

    Close · the controller signs

    Cash in 73 days, not 140

    The controller signs the close on working day 5. Person time on the order falls from 15.5 hours to about 35 minutes.

Illustrative figures from Meridian, the book’s fictional company. The threshold is p* = L ÷ (G + L). Book, Ch 30.3 and Ch 30.5

The same order in 2026 and at month 30, at your volume

The book prices the person time on this order before and after. Scale it to your own order volume and cost. Book, Ch 30.5
